body.p: Amendments in General

Claims 11 and 13 have been cancelled. Claim 1 has been amended to address informalities raised by the Office and to better define the subject matter therein. Similar amendments have been made to claim 18. Dependent claims 2-5, 8, 10, 12, and 15 have been amended for clarity purposes. New claims 19-25 have been added and are supported as discussed below. No new matter has been added.
Claim Objections

The Office has objected to claims 1, 4, 5, and 12 for informalities. While Applicant does not necessarily agree, Applicant submits that these issues have been resolved by the amendments to the claims.

The Office has rejected claims 1-5 and 8-18 under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) as being indefinite. While Applicant does not necessarily agree, Applicant submits that these rejections are moot in light of the amendments to the claims.

Claims 1-5 and 8-18 have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as being directed to a judicial exception, and more specifically, directed to an abstract idea. Applicant respectfully disagrees and requests that the Office reconsider, at least on the ground that
the claims are integrated into a practical application under Step 2A, Prong 2 of the analysis.
Step 2A, Prong 2 asks whether the claim recites additional element that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application. The Office argues on page 12 of the Office Action

that the claim elements do not "serve to apply the above-identified abstract idea with, or by use of, a particular machine." But this is not the case. Claims 1 and 18 explicitly recite an exercise machine, which is not a generic computer component. Numerous claim limitations are exercise-specific, such as values of exercise machine operating parameters, and suggestions of the multimedia content personal trainer. The claim provides exercisers with various options for their workout via a display module, including suggested options; and the recited exercise machine's settings are modified based on user selections. Moreover, claims 1 and 18 require "physically setting, by the data processing unit, the exercise machine based on the temporary controls made available by the control interface and selected by the user through the control interface in said first operating configuration." The settings of the exercise machine are being physically altered by selections made by a user. This is a practical application.

Indeed, the 2019 PEG actually supports the proposition that the claims are eligible under Step 2A, Prong 2, in Example 37 - Relocation of Icons on a Graphical User Interface. In that example, icons are rearranged on a graphical user interface (GUI) such that the most used icons are nearest the "start" icon of the computer system. There, the claim is eligible because "[t]he claim as a whole integrates the mental process into a practical application. Specifically, the additional elements recite a specific manner of

automatically displaying icons to the user based on usage which provides a specific improvement over prior systems, resulting in an improved user interface for electronic devices." Such is the case here-indeed, the recited claim limitations are an even more concrete practical application than that of Example 37. As described above, the claimed method uses the exercise machine components to provide, through a display interface, an improved and enhanced experience. As such, any judicial exception is integrated into a practical application such that the claims are eligible.

Moreover, the claim recites that the "exercise machine is a treadmill, a bike or exercise bike, a rowing machine, an indoor cycling machine, a strength exercise machine, or a station for practicing boxing." These are concrete, practical machines for use by exercisers.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant submits that the claims meet Step 2A, Prong 2 of the analysis, and requests the withdrawal of the rejection.
Claims 1-5 and 8-18 have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103
as being obvious over U.S. Pub. No. 2019/0336827 to Intonato et al. (hereinafter "Intonato") in view of U.S. Pub. No. 2019/0111318 to Evancha et al. (hereinafter "Evancha").
Claims 1 and 18 are independent claims from which all other claims depend, and as such the below arguments will focus upon these claims.
Claim 1 has been rejected as being obvious over Intonato in view of Evancha. Applicant respectfully disagrees and requests that the Office reconsider.

Claim 1 recites that "the step of dynamically modifying further comprises a step of indicating, by the data processing unit, based on the configuration instructions of the exercise machine read together with the playing of the multimedia content, wherein it is indicated on the display module which of the temporary controls representative of values selectable by the user of the at least one first operating parameter of the exercise machine is suggested by the personal trainer in the multimedia content for a phase of the set workout program that the user is performing in the set time interval that the multimedia content is at." One example of this limitation can be seen in FIG. 5b, where the arrows F1 indicate that the second temporary control V12 associated with a second value of the first operating parameter P1 is being suggested.
Notably, the claim recites "a plurality of temporary controls", i.e., there must be multiple temporary controls

available. This "plurality of temporary controls" is "simultaneously show[n] ."1 For example, in FIG. 5b the user can select V11, V12, V13, or V14; and V12 is being suggested as shown by the arrows F1. On page 21 of the Office Action, the Office cites paragraphs [0066] and [0069] of Intonato as disclosing an indicating step. However, Intonato is silent as to the display of multiple temporary controls as alternative options to one another, with a single temporary control being indicated as recommended.

1 In the Advisory Action of July 1, 2024, the Office stated Applicant was arguing a more narrow scope than actually claimed in this regard. While Applicant does not necessarily agree, the claim has now been amended to expressly recite a plurality of temporary controls that are shown simultaneously.
Nor does Evancha disclose such a limitation, whether taken alone or in combination with Intonato. Evancha discloses multiple

controls as shown on page 23 of the Office Action, but fails to disclose the indication of a suggestion of which control the user should select. There is no teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the Intonato/Evancha combination to display multiple alternative temporary controls as options, with one being indicated as suggested. As such, the claim is non-obvious.

New dependent claim 20 ultimately depends from independent claim 1, and thus is allowable for at least the same reasons. Moreover, Applicant submits that claim 20 is also allowable due to the additional limitations recited therein. For example, claim 20 recites a method "wherein the step of dynamically modifying comprises, in response to the user selecting a temporary control representative of initial workout difficulty level not suggested by the personal trainer, a step of removing, via the data processing unit, wherein the temporary controls representative of the initial workout difficulty levels selectable by the user on the display module other than the suggested temporary control are removed, and the temporary control representative of the initial workout difficulty level suggested by the personal trainer remains." Support for this limitation can be found, for example, in paragraph [0133] of U.S. Pub. No. 2021/0387073. With this method, the suggested temporary control remains available on the screen for the user to select it if they wish. Such a method is neither disclosed nor suggested by the Intonato/Evancha combination. As such, the claim is non-obvious.

New dependent claim 21 ultimately depends from independent claim 1, and thus is allowable for at least the same reasons. Moreover, Applicant submits that claim 21 is also allowable due to the additional limitations recited therein. For example, claim 21 recites a method "wherein the values selectable by the user of the at least one first operating parameter of the exercise machine are a function of an initial workout difficulty level selected by the user." Support for this limitation can be found, for example, in paragraph [0151] of U.S. Pub. No. 2021/0387073. With this method, the values of the displayed temporary controls are functions of the initial workout difficulty level selected by the user, thus providing the user more customized selections. Such a method is neither disclosed nor suggested by the Intonato/Evancha combination. As such, the claim is non-obvious.

New dependent claim 22 ultimately depends from independent claim 1, and thus is allowable for at least the same reasons. Moreover, Applicant submits that claim 22 is also allowable due to the additional limitations recited therein. For example, claim 22 recites a method "wherein which of the temporary controls representative of values selectable by the user of the at least one first operating parameter of the exercise machine is suggested is a function of an initial workout difficulty level selected by the user." Support for this limitation can be found, for example, in paragraph [0151] of U.S. Pub. No. 2021/0387073. With this method, the value of the suggested temporary control is a function of the initial workout difficulty level selected by the user, thus providing the user a more customized suggestion. Such a method is
neither disclosed nor suggested by the Intonato/Evancha combination. As such, the claim is non-obvious.

New dependent claim 23 ultimately depends from independent claim 1, and thus is allowable for at least the same reasons. Moreover, Applicant submits that claim 23 is also allowable due to the additional limitations recited therein. For example, claim 23 recites a method "wherein the value of the first operating parameter of at least one of the temporary controls is less than the value of the first operating parameter of the suggested temporary control, and the value of the first operating parameter of at least one of the temporary controls is greater than the value of the first operating parameter of the suggested temporary control." Support for this limitation can be found, for example, in FIG. 5b and associated portions of the specification of U.S. Pub. No. 2021/0387073. With this method, a user can select values either easier or harder than the value of the suggested temporary control. Such a method is neither disclosed nor suggested by the Intonato/Evancha combination. As such, the claim is non-obvious.

New dependent claim 24 ultimately depends from independent claim 1, and thus is allowable for at least the same reasons. Moreover, Applicant submits that claim 24 is also allowable due to the additional limitations recited therein. For example, claim 24 recites a method "wherein after an interval in which the user can select one of said values, if a value has not been selected, the value of the at least one first operating parameter suggested by the personal trainer is automatically selected." Support for this limitation can be found, for example, in paragraph [0159] of U.S.
Pub. No. 2021/0387073. Such a method is neither disclosed nor suggested by the Intonato/Evancha combination. As such, the claim is non-obvious.
Each of dependent claims 2-4, 7-12, 14-17, and 20-25 depends from allowable independent claim 1. As such, each of these claims is also non-obvious and allowable.

While different than independent claim 1, independent claim 18 contains similar limitations for which similar arguments apply. As such, Applicant submits that claim 18 is also non-obvious and allowable.

Dependent claim 19 depends from allowable independent claim 18. As such, this claim is also non-obvious and allowable. Moreover, claim 19 recites that "said at least one first operating parameter comprises: speed and/or slope of said treadmill;

resistance of said bike or exercise bike; resistance of said rowing machine; resistance of said indoor cycling machine; or resistance of said strength exercise machine." This further defines the exercise machine of claims 18 and 19 such that even if, arguendo, the claim recites an abstract idea, it is "appl[ied] . . . with, or by use of, a particular machine." As such, the claim recites patentable subject matter and should be allowed.

Although the present communication may include alterations to the application or claims, or characterizations of claim scope or referenced art, Applicant is not conceding in this application that previously pending claims are unpatentable over the cited references. Rather, any alterations or characterizations are being made to facilitate expeditious prosecution of this application.
Applicant submits that all claims pending herein are in condition for allowance and respectfully requests that a timely Notice of Allowance be issued in this case.
The Commissioner is hereby authorized to charge Deposit Account 60-2598 for any fees in connection with the prosecution of this application.
